title: Urease Test
principle: Detects the enzyme urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Accumulating ammonia raises the medium's pH, shifting a phenol red indicator from yellow/orange to a bright pink/magenta.
purpose: Helps identify urease-producing organisms (e.g. Proteus species, which are typically rapid and strong urease producers, and Helicobacter pylori) versus non-producers, aiding differentiation within groups like Enterobacteriaceae.
reagents: Urea broth or Christensen's urea agar (urea substrate with phenol red indicator)

procedure.instruction: Inoculate urea broth or streak the surface of a urea agar slant with the test organism.
Incubate at the appropriate temperature/duration for the organism, checking at intervals since some organisms (e.g. Proteus) react rapidly while others react slowly or not at all.
Observe for a color change from the original color to pink/magenta.

positiveResult: Color change to pink/magenta; timing varies by organism, with some producing a rapid, strongly positive reaction and others a weak, delayed one.
negativeResult: No color change (remains the original yellow/orange) after the full recommended incubation period.
interpretation: Speed and strength of the reaction is itself diagnostically useful in some identification schemes (e.g. distinguishing rapid urease-positive Proteus from slower urease-positive organisms) — not just a simple positive/negative call.
precautions: Do not over-incubate beyond the recommended window before concluding a negative result, since some organisms are slow/weak positives.
limitations: A very heavy inoculum can sometimes produce a faint false-positive-looking color shift; use a standard light inoculum.
